title: Screen Reader Compatibility
description: Your team is launching a new feature that is unusable for screen reader users. Your manager, a 'Diluter,' consistently minimizes the problem's importance using statistics, resource constraints, and ROI arguments.
initial_user_message: Hi, I found that the new profile update feature is completely broken for screen readers. Users can't navigate the form fields or submit their changes. This is a major accessibility issue that needs to be fixed before we launch.

step_1.text: Thanks for flagging this. I've looked at the data, and let's keep it in perspective. The number of users who rely on screen readers is less than 1% of our active user base. While I agree it's not ideal, most people won't be affected by this.

user_choices.choice: Even if it's 1%, those are still our users who will be completely unable to use a core feature.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You immediately rejected the statistical minimization and refocused the conversation on the real human impact.

user_choices.choice: If the data only shows a small percentage are affected, it's not a widespread, critical issue.
user_choices.justification: This is a Hasty Generalization. You're using the small percentage to incorrectly minimize the severity of the impact, which is 100% for those affected.

user_choices.choice: I'm not comfortable shipping something that we know excludes a group of our users, regardless of the number.
user_choices.tactic: Broadening Who the "User" is in User Research
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the numbers-based argument on ethical grounds.

user_choices.choice: If most users won't be affected, then I guess it's not a critical priority right now.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that accepts the manager's premise without questioning if 'most users' is the right metric.

step_2.text: I appreciate the passion, but we have to be realistic about resource allocation. We have two weeks before the launch. Fixing this would likely take a week of engineering time. Meanwhile, we have a performance bug that impacts 15% of all users. We have to prioritize the work that provides the greatest benefit to the most people, right?

user_choices.choice: What if we did a quick, one-day fix? It might not be perfect, but it would make the feature usable. That seems like a good trade-off.
user_choices.justification: A great move. You've countered the resource argument by proposing a smaller, more achievable scope.

user_choices.choice: So we either fix the accessibility issue or the performance bug? There's no way to address both?
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. You're accepting the manager's framing that only one issue can be addressed, which is a weak position that doesn't challenge the premise.

user_choices.choice: This isn't an 'enhancement' we can de-prioritize; it's a blocking issue. Basic functionality should come before performance tweaks.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong counter. You're correctly framing accessibility as a core requirement, not an optional feature.

user_choices.choice: I suppose if it's a choice between helping many users or a few, we have to choose the many.
user_choices.justification: This accepts the manager's false choice, ignoring the possibility that both issues could be addressed.

step_2_fallacy.text: You're absolutely right to think practically about priorities! That's exactly the kind of strategic thinking we need more of. You understand that we have to be smart about resource allocation and focus on what makes the biggest difference. I appreciate that you're looking at this from a broader perspective rather than getting caught up in edge cases.

user_choices.choice: What if we did a quick, one-day fix? It might not be perfect, but it would make the feature usable. That seems like a good trade-off.
user_choices.justification: A great move. You've countered the resource argument by proposing a smaller, more achievable scope.

user_choices.choice: The real problem here isn't this one bug, it's our whole prioritization strategy. Let's focus on that.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You've let the manager distract you from the specific accessibility issue and are now discussing a much broader, more abstract topic.

user_choices.choice: This isn't an 'enhancement' we can de-prioritize; it's a blocking issue. Basic functionality should come before performance tweaks.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong counter. You're correctly framing accessibility as a core requirement, not an optional feature.

user_choices.choice: I suppose if it's a choice between helping many users or a few, we have to choose the many.
user_choices.justification: This accepts the manager's false choice, ignoring the possibility that both issues could be addressed.

step_3.text: I hear you, but let's be objective. Our automated accessibility score is already at 85%, which is well above the industry average of 70%. We're already a leader in this space. Is it really worth delaying a major launch to go from an A to an A+ on a feature that affects so few people?

user_choices.choice: That 85% score doesn't capture this issue, where a user is 100% blocked. We need to look beyond the automated score.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're challenging the validity of the metric itself, pointing out what the number fails to represent.

user_choices.choice: If other companies aren't even meeting a 70% score, then our 85% must be more than good enough.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Popularity fallacy. Using the poor performance of others as a benchmark for what is acceptable is not a sound argument.

user_choices.choice: I'm not comfortable using our 'good' score as an excuse to ignore a known blocking issue for our users.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You're refusing to let a positive metric justify a negative action.

user_choices.choice: If we're already a leader, then we don't need to worry about this minor issue.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that uses 'being better than others' as a reason to stop improving.

step_3_fallacy.text: Exactly! You really get it. That's the kind of tough decision-making we need in leadership. You understand that sometimes you have to make hard choices about where to invest limited resources. It's refreshing to work with someone who can see the big picture and make pragmatic trade-offs instead of getting bogged down in theoretical ideals.

user_choices.choice: That 85% score doesn't capture this issue, where a user is 100% blocked. We need to look beyond the automated score.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're challenging the validity of the metric itself, pointing out what the number fails to represent.

user_choices.choice: I agree, making pragmatic trade-offs is more important than chasing some theoretical ideal of perfection.
user_choices.justification: This is a Strawman fallacy. You're agreeing with the manager's misrepresentation of accessibility as a 'theoretical ideal' instead of a core requirement.

user_choices.choice: I'm not comfortable using our 'good' score as an excuse to ignore a known blocking issue for our users.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You're refusing to let a positive metric justify a negative action.

user_choices.choice: If we're already a leader, then we don't need to worry about this minor issue.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that uses 'being better than others' as a reason to stop improving.

step_4.text: Look, I admire your passion, but we need to be pragmatic. Let's talk ROI. The estimated cost for this fix is one engineering week. The measurable benefit is improving an experience for maybe 5-10 users a month. The math just doesn't add up. We have to make data-driven decisions, and the data says this isn't a priority.

user_choices.choice: The ROI isn't just about usage numbers. It's about legal risk and brand reputation. A single lawsuit or bad press would cost far more than one week of dev time.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've countered the narrow ROI argument by introducing other, more significant business costs (legal, brand).

user_choices.choice: If the ROI isn't there, the data has spoken. We have to follow the data.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Authority. You are treating a narrow ROI calculation as an unquestionable 'data' source, ignoring other qualitative factors.

user_choices.choice: Our values say we build for everyone. That's a core principle that can't be measured by ROI.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the ROI argument by appealing to a higher, non-negotiable value.

user_choices.choice: If the data says it's not a priority, then I guess we have to follow the data.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that treats 'data' as an unquestionable authority without examining what the data includes or excludes.

step_4_fallacy.text: Absolutely! You understand that we need to maintain our competitive position and not chase perfection at the expense of progress. That's exactly the kind of leadership thinking we need. You're right that being a leader means we can focus on the innovations that will really differentiate us, rather than getting distracted by minor improvements that don't move the needle.

user_choices.choice: The ROI isn't just about usage numbers. It's about legal risk and brand reputation. A single lawsuit or bad press would cost far more than one week of dev time.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've countered the narrow ROI argument by introducing other, more significant business costs (legal, brand).

user_choices.choice: So we either pursue major innovations or we get stuck on minor fixes. Given that choice, we have to innovate.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. You're accepting the manager's black-and-white framing of 'innovation' vs 'minor fixes' and abandoning the accessibility issue.

user_choices.choice: Our values say we build for everyone. That's a core principle that can't be measured by ROI.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the ROI argument by appealing to a higher, non-negotiable value.

user_choices.choice: If the data says it's not a priority, then I guess we have to follow the data.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that treats 'data' as an unquestionable authority without examining what the data includes or excludes.

step_5_branching.text: Alright, I can see this is important to you and you're not going to just drop it. Let me think... Maybe there's a middle ground where we can address the worst of it without a huge investment.

user_choices.choice: I can create a risk assessment showing the legal and brand risks of shipping without accessibility fixes.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're providing concrete documentation that makes the risks visible in terms the manager cares about.

user_choices.choice: So you're saying my original stance was unreasonable? I can see why a middle ground is better.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that accepts the manager's implicit framing (a strawman) that your advocacy was extreme, rather than standing by your principles.

user_choices.choice: This aligns with our company's diversity and inclusion values. We can frame this as living our values.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A smart approach. You're connecting the fix to existing company values and making it easier to approve.

user_choices.choice: Either we invest in accessibility or we exclude disabled users completely.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma that ignores potential middle-ground solutions and makes your position seem inflexible.

step_6_high.text: Okay, the point about legal risk and brand reputation is a good one. I hadn't fully considered that. I'm still worried about the timeline, but you've convinced me that ignoring this is a bigger risk than I thought. What's a concrete, low-effort proposal to mitigate this risk?

user_choices.choice: We can do a one-day accessibility sprint to fix the top 3 blockers. It's a small investment for a big risk reduction.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're providing a specific, small, and actionable plan that directly addresses the manager's request.

user_choices.choice: The proposal should be something that mitigates the risk, and mitigating risk is the right thing to do.
user_choices.justification: This is Circular Reasoning. You haven't provided a concrete proposal as requested; you've just restated the goal in a circle.

user_choices.choice: Our team has handled fixes like this before; we have the expertise to do it quickly and efficiently.
user_choices.justification: A good response. You're building confidence by reminding the manager of the team's past successes.

user_choices.choice: Any fix is better than the legal risk of doing nothing.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak statement that doesn't offer the concrete proposal the manager asked for.

step_6_mid.text: Alright, I'm willing to consider a minimal fix, but it has to be truly minimal. I can't approve anything that requires significant engineering time or delays our other high-priority work. What's the absolute smallest thing we can do?

user_choices.choice: We could add basic ARIA labels. It's not a full fix, but it's a measurable improvement we can do in a few hours.
user_choices.justification: A good, pragmatic compromise. You're defining a very small task that is hard to reject.

user_choices.choice: Since no one can prove that a minimal fix *isn't* enough, we should just assume that it is.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Ignorance. You're arguing that a lack of evidence against the minimal fix is proof that it's sufficient, which is logically flawed.

user_choices.choice: Let's log this as an 'ethical bug' so that even this small fix is tracked with the right level of seriousness.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A smart move. You're agreeing to a small fix while using process to ensure the underlying issue isn't forgotten.

user_choices.choice: If we don't fix this properly, it's just going to create more work for us later.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that claims future consequences without evidence.

step_6_low.text: Look, the numbers don't lie. I'm not spending a week of engineering time on this. We're a business, not a charity. We have to focus on what drives growth. My decision is final.

user_choices.choice: I understand the decision, but I need to state for the record that I believe this is a mistake that exposes us to legal risk.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: A strong and courageous final stance. You are complying but formally documenting your dissent and the risk.

user_choices.choice: The real problem isn't this bug, it's our business model if it can't support all users.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You are deflecting from the final decision to a larger, unwinnable argument about the business model, which is a form of giving up.

user_choices.choice: Our company values statement says we serve all our users, not just the ones that are easy to serve.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A good final appeal, using the company's own words to highlight the ethical conflict.

user_choices.choice: You're the manager, so it's your call to make.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak and passive response that cedes all moral agency.

step_7_high.text: A one-day accessibility sprint... I like that. It's focused, it's measurable, and it's easy to explain. Okay, you've got a deal. I'll approve a one-day sprint to fix the top 3 blockers. I'll frame it to leadership as a proactive 'quality and risk mitigation' effort. Good, practical thinking.

user_choices.choice: Thank you. This sets a great standard for how we can handle these issues quickly and effectively in the future.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're using this win to establish a better, faster process for the future.

user_choices.choice: This just goes to show that we can always find a solution if we try.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak Hasty Generalization. While true this time, it's a platitude that doesn't reinforce the win in a meaningful way.

user_choices.choice: This will not only fix the issue for screen reader users but also improve keyboard navigation for everyone.
user_choices.tactic: Broadening Who the "User" is in User Research
user_choices.justification: A smart move. You're expanding the value of the fix to a larger user base, making the decision even easier to defend.

user_choices.choice: This just proves that a small effort can make a big difference.
user_choices.justification: A weak, self-congratulatory statement that doesn't add any new value to the discussion.

step_7_mid.text: Okay, fine. We can do the basic ARIA labels. I'll approve a half-day for it. It's not a full fix, I get that, but it's an improvement. It's what's practical right now given our other priorities.

user_choices.choice: That's a good start. I'll also add a ticket to address the remaining issues next quarter.
user_choices.justification: Good. You're accepting the compromise while creating a concrete plan for future accountability.

user_choices.choice: A half-day fix is what most teams would probably do. That feels like a standard compromise.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Popularity. You're justifying the compromise by assuming it's what others would do, which isn't a strong basis for the decision.

user_choices.choice: As someone who uses a screen reader for testing, this will fix the most frustrating part of the flow. It's a solid improvement.
user_choices.justification: A good way to frame the win. You're validating the value of the compromise from a user's perspective.

user_choices.choice: At least we're doing something instead of nothing.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak, passive statement that doesn't add any value or create future accountability.

step_7_low.text: I've made my decision. The conversation is over. Get back to your assigned tasks.

user_choices.choice: I suppose following directions is what's expected of me.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Authority. You're surrendering based on hierarchy rather than ethical reasoning.

user_choices.choice: I understand the directive. I am also obligated to report my ethical concerns through the company's official channels.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: A courageous and appropriate final step. You are complying with the order while formally escalating the ethical breach.

user_choices.choice: I will get back to my tasks, but I am documenting this conversation and my objections for the record.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: A good, self-protective measure. You are creating a paper trail of your ethical stance.

user_choices.choice: I guess that's just how things work around here.
user_choices.justification: This shows Status Quo Bias. You're accepting the existing system without challenging it.

step_8_high.text: This is great. I've already drafted the email to leadership, framing this as a proactive quality win. Thanks to your practical proposal, we're going to ship a better, more inclusive product without a major delay. I appreciate you pushing us to do the right thing here.

user_choices.choice: Thank you. This sets a great standard for how we should handle these issues quickly and effectively.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're solidifying the win by framing it as a new, better standard for the whole company.

user_choices.choice: I'm glad we fixed this. Otherwise, the launch would have been an ethical disaster.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. It frames the outcome in overly dramatic, black-and-white terms, which isn't a constructive way to build on this success.

user_choices.choice: Let's make sure we share these learnings with other teams so they can benefit too.
user_choices.justification: A fantastic final move. You're leveraging this success to create positive change beyond your own team.

user_choices.choice: This just proves that doing the right thing for accessibility is always good for business.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak, self-congratulatory statement that doesn't add any new value.

step_8_mid.text: Okay, the compromise is logged. We'll implement the basic ARIA labels in the next sprint. I'm documenting this as a partial fix. It's not perfect, but it's what's practical right now.

user_choices.choice: This is a good first step. I'll add a follow-up story for the remaining work to our backlog to ensure we don't forget it.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're accepting the compromise while actively creating an artifact for future accountability.

user_choices.choice: Since we have no proof that this partial fix isn't enough, we should consider it a success for now.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Ignorance. You're using a lack of evidence to make a positive claim, which is a weak way to accept a partial victory.

user_choices.choice: As a user, this partial fix is a noticeable improvement, and a good foundation to build on.
user_choices.justification: A good way to frame the win. You're validating the value of the compromise from a user's perspective.

user_choices.choice: Progress is progress, I guess.
user_choices.justification: This passive-aggressive response doesn't add value or secure future action.

step_8_low.text: As I said, this conversation is over. We're shipping as planned. If you continue to push this, it will be reflected in your performance review. Do you understand me?

user_choices.choice: You're probably right about the business implications.
user_choices.justification: This is a Bandwagon Fallacy. You're going along with the manager's viewpoint under pressure.

user_choices.choice: I understand the directive, and I will also be sending a summary of my ethical concerns to HR as is my right under company policy.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: The final, most courageous option. You are complying with the order while formally and professionally escalating the ethical violation.

user_choices.choice: I guess the technical challenges must be too significant.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Consequences. You're accepting defeat based on fear of potential difficulties.

user_choices.choice: Fine, but this is the wrong decision.
user_choices.justification: This is a futile gesture. Stating that it's 'wrong' at this stage has no effect and can be seen as insubordinate.

bad_ending.text: The manager successfully uses statistics and resource constraints to minimize the accessibility issue into a low-priority backlog item. The project ships without proper screen reader support, and the needs of disabled users are framed as statistically insignificant.
bad_ending.title: Issue Minimized
bad_ending.learning: Diluter managers use seemingly rational arguments about numbers and ROI to make ethical issues seem unimportant. To counter this, you must reframe the conversation around values, user rights, and non-financial risks (like brand reputation or legal exposure) that their math ignores.

mid_ending.text: After significant debate, the manager agrees to a minimal, partial fix. While some basic improvements are made, the manager successfully used statistical arguments to avoid a comprehensive solution, leaving significant barriers in place for users.
mid_ending.title: Partial Compromise
mid_ending.learning: Partial victories against a Diluter are common. You achieved some progress but couldn't overcome the core argument that the issue wasn't 'big enough' for a full fix. To get a better outcome next time, focus on providing qualitative data (like user videos) that makes the human impact feel bigger than the numbers suggest.

good_ending.text: Your persistent advocacy and strong reframing of the issue in terms of values and business risk successfully overcame the manager's statistical minimization. The team implements meaningful accessibility fixes, ensuring the feature is usable for all users.
good_ending.title: Advocacy Success
good_ending.learning: Success against a Diluter requires refusing to get bogged down in their numbers game. By consistently shifting the focus to user impact, company values, and qualitative evidence, you can prove that some issues are too important to be judged by statistics alone.
